claim: Coordination of cell growth with division is essential for proper cell function.
source: Coordination of cell growth with division is essential for proper cell function.
evidence: This is a general statement about cell biology that represents established scientific knowledge.

claim: A mechanism controlling bud size in G2/M prevents premature onset of anaphase and controls the overall size variability.
source: Our analysis establishes the existence of a mechanism controlling bud size in G2/M that prevents premature onset of anaphase, and controls the overall size variability.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, particularly in Figure 3 and related analyses.

claim: Most G1 mutants do not display impaired size homeostasis.
source: While most G1 mutants do not display impaired size homeostasis, mutants in which cyclin B-Cdk regulation is altered display large size variability.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from mutant analysis shown in Figures 4 and 6.

claim: Mutants in which cyclin B-Cdk regulation is altered display large size variability.
source: While most G1 mutants do not display impaired size homeostasis, mutants in which cyclin B-Cdk regulation is altered display large size variability.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from mutant analysis shown in Figures 4 and 6.

claim: Size homeostasis is not controlled by a G1-specific mechanism alone but is likely to be an emergent property resulting from the integration of several mechanisms that coordinate cell and bud growth with division.
source: Our study thus demonstrates that size homeostasis is not controlled by a G1-specific mechanism alone but is likely to be an emergent property resulting from the integration of several mechanisms that coordinate cell and bud growth with division.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the integration of multiple experimental observations throughout the study.

claim: A 'Sizer' mechanism operates in yeast where the transition to a given cell cycle phase occurs when cells have attained a critical size during the preceding phase.
source: In contrast, a 'Sizer' mechanism has been shown to operate in yeast: the transition to a given cell cycle phase (resp. mitotic entry in fission yeast and DNA replication in budding yeast) occurs when cells have attained a critical size during the preceding phase (resp. G2 phase in fission yeast and G1 in budding yeast) (Fantes, 1977; Fantes and Nurse, 1977).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work by Fantes and colleagues.

claim: Pom1 deletion does not alter size homeostasis in fission yeast.
source: Later studies disproved this model, by showing in particular that Pom1 deletion does not alter size homeostasis, as would be expected following disruption of a core player in the size signaling pathway (Bhatia et al., 2014; Wood and Nurse, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies by Bhatia et al. and Wood and Nurse.

claim: The nuclear concentration of Whi5 is larger in small daughter cells compared with large mother cells at birth.
source: Alternatively, recent work showed that the concentration of Whi5, a major inhibitor of G1/S cyclin expression, is gradually diluted during G1 but is synthesized in a cell size-independent manner during S/G2/M phases; thus, the nuclear concentration of Whi5 is larger in small daughter cells compared with the large mother cells at birth (Schmoller et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Schmoller et al., 2015.

claim: The WHI5 mutant displays a small cell size phenotype.
source: Nevertheless, although the WHI5 mutant displays a small cell size phenotype (Jorgensen et al., 2002), the G1 size-compensation effect is reduced but not abolished (Soifer et al., 2016; Turner et al., 2012), and the overall width of the cell size distribution of Whi5 mutants and wild-type (WT) yeast are similar (Jorgensen et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Jorgensen et al., 2002.

claim: The G1 size-compensation effect is reduced but not abolished in WHI5 mutants.
source: Nevertheless, although the WHI5 mutant displays a small cell size phenotype (Jorgensen et al., 2002), the G1 size-compensation effect is reduced but not abolished (Soifer et al., 2016; Turner et al., 2012), and the overall width of the cell size distribution of Whi5 mutants and wild-type (WT) yeast are similar (Jorgensen et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Soifer et al., 2016 and Turner et al., 2012.

claim: whi5Δ mutants display compensatory growth in S/G2/M.
source: whi5Δ mutants and cells carrying other genetic perturbations that induce a premature G1/S transition also display compensatory growth in S/G2/M (Charvin et al., 2009; Harvey and Kellogg, 2003; Soifer and Barkai, 2014), which is analogous to the 'cryptic' G1/S size control observed long ago in wee1Δ fission yeast (Fantes, 1981).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Charvin et al., 2009, Harvey and Kellogg, 2003, and Soifer and Barkai, 2014.

claim: Bacteria reach size homeostasis through an 'Adder' mechanism, whereby a constant amount of cellular material is added at every cell cycle.
source: Recent observations in bacteria proposed that a size-compensation mechanism may not even be necessary to ensure cell homeostasis. In contrast to a Sizer mechanism, in which cell size variation during the cell cycle is negatively correlated with the initial cell size, bacteria passively reach size homeostasis through an 'Adder' mechanism, whereby a constant amount of cellular material is added at every cell cycle (Campos et al., 2014; Jun and Taheri-Araghi, 2015; Taheri-Araghi et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Campos et al., 2014, Jun and Taheri-Araghi, 2015, and Taheri-Araghi et al., 2015.

claim: The burst of histone synthesis is tightly coupled to DNA replication.
source: We reasoned that the burst of histone synthesis could serve as an accurate marker of S phase, thanks to the tight reciprocal coupling of DNA replication and histone synthesis, which has been characterized in detail (Baumbach et al., 1987; Heintz et al., 1983; Nelson et al., 2002; Sittman et al., 1983).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies on histone synthesis and DNA replication coupling.

claim: HTB2-sfGFP fluorescence shows a ~2-fold enrichment in histones before compared with after the histone synthesis phase.
source: Quantification of fluorescence levels gave a consistent ~2-fold enrichment in histones before compared with after the histone synthesis phase (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E and F), as expected by the doubling of DNA content.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2E and F.

claim: HTB2-sfGFP fluorescence is evenly partitioned between mother and daughter cells upon nuclear division with a D/M asymmetry of 0.94 ± 0.01.
source: Similarly, we verified that HTB2-sfGFP fluorescence was evenly partitioned between mother and daughter cells upon nuclear division (Daughter/Mother [D/M] asymmetry = 0.94 ± 0.01 Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The GFP-tag at the HTB2 locus only modestly affects cell division.
source: We observed that the GFP-tag at the HTB2 locus only modestly affected cell division (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–C.

claim: The maturation time of mCherry is ~45 min.
source: A numerical model confirmed that this effect could be quantitatively explained by the much longer maturation time of mCherry (~45 min [Charvin et al., 2008]) compared with sfGFP (~5 min [Pédelacq et al., 2006]), which blurs the apparent dynamics of histone synthesis (Figure 1—figure supplement 4E–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Charvin et al., 2008.

claim: The maturation time of sfGFP is ~5 min.
source: A numerical model confirmed that this effect could be quantitatively explained by the much longer maturation time of mCherry (~45 min [Charvin et al., 2008]) compared with sfGFP (~5 min [Pédelacq et al., 2006]), which blurs the apparent dynamics of histone synthesis (Figure 1—figure supplement 4E–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Pédelacq et al., 2006.

claim: Cytokinesis and nuclear division are tightly correlated with a Pearson coefficient of 0.94.
source: We measured that cytokinesis (the sudden drop in Cdc10-mCherry fluorescence) and nuclear division were tightly correlated (Pearson coefficient 0.94), with a median offset of 5.6 ± 0.4 min between both events (Figure 1—figure supplement 5D and Figure 1—figure supplement 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5D and E.

claim: There is a median offset of 5.6 ± 0.4 min between nuclear division and cytokinesis.
source: We measured that cytokinesis (the sudden drop in Cdc10-mCherry fluorescence) and nuclear division were tightly correlated (Pearson coefficient 0.94), with a median offset of 5.6 ± 0.4 min between both events (Figure 1—figure supplement 5D and Figure 1—figure supplement 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5D and E.

claim: Start consistently occurs before the onset of histone synthesis.
source: Start consistently occurred before the onset of histone synthesis (Fig. Figure 1—figure supplement 5I–J), which was expected because HTB2 expression is controlled by the G1/S-specific transcription factors SBF/MBF.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5I–J and knowledge about HTB2 regulation.

claim: 63% of collected wild-type cell cycles passed the quality control procedure.
source: By pooling 17 replicate experiments, we collected ~26,900 cell cycles for WT cells (Figure 1C) of which 63% passed our quality control procedure aimed at discarding cells with segmentation/tracking or data fitting issues (see Supporting Information and Figure 1—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the data processing results.

claim: For wild-type mother cells, G1 duration is 19.0 ± 0.1 min.
source: Thus, the durations for mothers and daughters, respectively, were: G1 (19.0 ± 0.1 and 45.5 ± 0.3 min) (Di Talia et al., 2007), S (29.5 ± 0.1 and 36.7 ± 0.2 min) (Magiera et al., 2014), G2/M (15.7 ± 0.1 and 14.7 ± 0.1 min), and Ana (11.4 ± 0.1 and 12.2 ± 0.1 min), Figure 1D and supplementary file 2.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and supplementary file 2.

claim: For wild-type daughter cells, G1 duration is 45.5 ± 0.3 min.
source: Thus, the durations for mothers and daughters, respectively, were: G1 (19.0 ± 0.1 and 45.5 ± 0.3 min) (Di Talia et al., 2007), S (29.5 ± 0.1 and 36.7 ± 0.2 min) (Magiera et al., 2014), G2/M (15.7 ± 0.1 and 14.7 ± 0.1 min), and Ana (11.4 ± 0.1 and 12.2 ± 0.1 min), Figure 1D and supplementary file 2.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and supplementary file 2.

claim: For wild-type mother cells, S phase duration is 29.5 ± 0.1 min.
source: Thus, the durations for mothers and daughters, respectively, were: G1 (19.0 ± 0.1 and 45.5 ± 0.3 min) (Di Talia et al., 2007), S (29.5 ± 0.1 and 36.7 ± 0.2 min) (Magiera et al., 2014), G2/M (15.7 ± 0.1 and 14.7 ± 0.1 min), and Ana (11.4 ± 0.1 and 12.2 ± 0.1 min), Figure 1D and supplementary file 2.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and supplementary file 2.

claim: For wild-type daughter cells, S phase duration is 36.7 ± 0.2 min.
source: Thus, the durations for mothers and daughters, respectively, were: G1 (19.0 ± 0.1 and 45.5 ± 0.3 min) (Di Talia et al., 2007), S (29.5 ± 0.1 and 36.7 ± 0.2 min) (Magiera et al., 2014), G2/M (15.7 ± 0.1 and 14.7 ± 0.1 min), and Ana (11.4 ± 0.1 and 12.2 ± 0.1 min), Figure 1D and supplementary file 2.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and supplementary file 2.

claim: The S phase is 7.2 min longer in daughters compared with young mother cells.
source: For instance, the S phase was 7.2 min longer in daughters compared with young mother cells (p<0.001; Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D with statistical significance.

claim: S phase duration converges toward an asymptotic value over several divisions following cell birth.
source: In addition, this interval converged toward an asymptotic value over several divisions following cell birth (Figure 1—figure supplement 9).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 9.

claim: G1 duration decreases abruptly when daughters become mother cells in their subsequent division.
source: This contrasts with G1 duration, which decreased abruptly when daughters (replicative age 0, Figure 1—figure supplement 9) became mother cells (replicative age >0, Figure 1—figure supplement 9) in their subsequent division, and G2/M, the duration of which is quite independent of the replicative age of the cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 9.

claim: G2/M duration is quite independent of the replicative age of the cells.
source: This contrasts with G1 duration, which decreased abruptly when daughters (replicative age 0, Figure 1—figure supplement 9) became mother cells (replicative age >0, Figure 1—figure supplement 9) in their subsequent division, and G2/M, the duration of which is quite independent of the replicative age of the cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 9.

claim: Hydroxyurea induces a progressive concentration-dependent increase in S phase duration in both mother and daughter cells.
source: As expected, we observed a progressive HU concentration-dependent increase in S phase duration in both mother and daughter cells, from an average of 27.1 ± 0.4 min and 35.1 ± 0.8 min at 0 mM to 48.0 ± 1.4 and 43.9 ± 1.4 min at 50 mM HU, respectively (p<0.001, Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Hydroxyurea treatment causes a doubling in G2/M duration from ~15 min to ~30 min in both mothers and daughters.
source: This prolongation of S phase was accompanied by a parallel doubling in G2/M duration (from ~15 min to ~30 min in both mothers and daughters, p<0.001, Figure 2A), which is likely due to the activation of the checkpoint that follows DNA damage(Weinert et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and citation to Weinert et al., 1994.

claim: sic1 and whi5 daughter cells undergo premature entry into S phase compared with WT cells.
source: First, we confirmed that sic1 and whi5 (G1/S transition repressors) daughter cells underwent premature entry into S phase (i.e., shorter G1 duration) compared with WT cells (Soifer and Barkai, 2014), which was accompanied by a compensatory increase in G2/M duration (Figure 2B) (Soifer and Barkai, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and citation to Soifer and Barkai, 2014.

claim: Premature entry into S phase in sic1 and whi5 mutants is accompanied by a compensatory increase in G2/M duration.
source: First, we confirmed that sic1 and whi5 (G1/S transition repressors) daughter cells underwent premature entry into S phase (i.e., shorter G1 duration) compared with WT cells (Soifer and Barkai, 2014), which was accompanied by a compensatory increase in G2/M duration (Figure 2B) (Soifer and Barkai, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and citation to Soifer and Barkai, 2014.

claim: Mutation of BCK2 causes a small delay in G1 of daughter cells.
source: Conversely, mutation of G1/S transition activator BCK2 (Soifer and Barkai, 2014), but not CLN3, caused a small delay in G1 of daughter cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citation to Soifer and Barkai, 2014.

claim: Deletion of SWE1 induces a slight increase in G1 duration of daughter cells.
source: We found that deletion of SWE1, a kinase that inhibits Cyclin B/Cdk activity and therefore prevents a premature onset of anaphase, did barely affect G2/M duration, yet induced a slight increase in G1 duration of daughter cells, as previously observed (Harvey and Kellogg, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citation to Harvey and Kellogg, 2003.

claim: Mutants defective in Hcm1 display longer G2/M phases.
source: However, mutants defective in Hcm1, a forkhead transcription factor that regulates late S phase genes, or Clb2, one of the main mitotic cyclins, both displayed longer G2/M phases (Figure 2D), in agreement with previous measurements (Pramila et al., 2006; Surana et al., 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D and citations to Pramila et al., 2006 and Surana et al., 1991.

claim: Mutants defective in Clb2 display longer G2/M phases.
source: However, mutants defective in Hcm1, a forkhead transcription factor that regulates late S phase genes, or Clb2, one of the main mitotic cyclins, both displayed longer G2/M phases (Figure 2D), in agreement with previous measurements (Pramila et al., 2006; Surana et al., 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D and citations to Pramila et al., 2006 and Surana et al., 1991.

claim: There is a negative correlation between size at birth and the duration of G1 in daughter cells.
source: This analysis successfully confirmed classical results, such as the negative correlation between size at birth (Vbirth) and the duration of G1 (TG1) in daughter cells (yellow star in Figure 3B) (Di Talia et al., 2007), which is indicative of a G1 compensatory mechanism in small daughter cells, as well as the positive correlation between the growth rate in unbudded cells (μunb.) and the cell volume the end of G1 (VG1) in daughters cells (green star in Figure 3B)(Ferrezuelo et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and citation to Di Talia et al., 2007.

claim: There is a positive correlation between the growth rate in unbudded cells and the cell volume at the end of G1 in daughter cells.
source: This analysis successfully confirmed classical results, such as the negative correlation between size at birth (Vbirth) and the duration of G1 (TG1) in daughter cells (yellow star in Figure 3B) (Di Talia et al., 2007), which is indicative of a G1 compensatory mechanism in small daughter cells, as well as the positive correlation between the growth rate in unbudded cells (μunb.) and the cell volume the end of G1 (VG1) in daughters cells (green star in Figure 3B)(Ferrezuelo et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and citation to Ferrezuelo et al., 2012.

claim: The duration of G2/M varies inversely with the volume of the bud at the end of S phase in both mother and daughter cells.
source: However, this analysis also revealed that the duration of G2/M (TG2/M) varies inversely with the volume of the bud at the end of S phase (VbS) in both mother and daughter cells, see magenta stars in Figure 3B.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: After reaching the end of S phase, cells experience a bud size–dependent delay before entering anaphase.
source: This suggest that, after reaching the end of S phase, cells experience a bud size–dependent delay before entering anaphase.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed negative correlation between G2/M duration and bud size at the end of S phase.

claim: Wild-type daughter cells display a G1 size compensation slope of sG1 = -0.30 ± 0.01.
source: The analysis captured the well-characterized daughter-specific Sizer in G1 (Figure 3D: slope sG1 is negative in daughters, −0.30 ± 0.01, but approaches zero in mothers, −0.02 ± 0.01) (Di Talia et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Wild-type mother cells display a G1 size compensation slope of sG1 = -0.02 ± 0.01.
source: The analysis captured the well-characterized daughter-specific Sizer in G1 (Figure 3D: slope sG1 is negative in daughters, −0.30 ± 0.01, but approaches zero in mothers, −0.02 ± 0.01) (Di Talia et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Daughter cells behave as a weak Sizer over the entire cell cycle with stot = -0.22 ± 0.02.
source: It also confirmed that the daughter and the mother cells behave as a weak Sizer and Adder, respectively, over the entire cell cycle (stot = −0.22 ± 0.02 for daughters and 0.09 ± 0.01 for mothers) – in previous studies, the low absolute values of stot showed that the budding yeast cell cycle behaves as an Adder, as observed in other unicellular organisms (Jun and Taheri-Araghi, 2015; Soifer et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citations to Jun and Taheri-Araghi, 2015 and Soifer et al., 2016.

claim: Mother cells behave as an Adder over the entire cell cycle with stot = 0.09 ± 0.01.
source: It also confirmed that the daughter and the mother cells behave as a weak Sizer and Adder, respectively, over the entire cell cycle (stot = −0.22 ± 0.02 for daughters and 0.09 ± 0.01 for mothers) – in previous studies, the low absolute values of stot showed that the budding yeast cell cycle behaves as an Adder, as observed in other unicellular organisms (Jun and Taheri-Araghi, 2015; Soifer et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citations to Jun and Taheri-Araghi, 2015 and Soifer et al., 2016.

claim: There is a bud-specific size-compensatory growth in G2/M with sG2/M = -0.39 ± 0.01 in daughters and -0.49 ± 0.01 in mothers.
source: In addition, the data clearly indicated the existence of a bud-specific size-compensatory growth in G2/M in both daughter and mother cells (sG2/M = −0.39 ± 0.01 and −0.49 ± 0.01 in daughters and mothers, respectively, Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The magnitude of the G2/M bud size control is comparable to the G1 size control.
source: Therefore, these results suggest that at least two mechanisms may act coordinately to ensure size homeostasis throughout the cell cycle (Soifer and Barkai, 2014).
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of size compensation slopes in G1 and G2/M phases.

claim: Deletion of Whi5 decreases the magnitude of G1 control to sG1 = -0.17 ± 0.02.
source: We found that deletion of the repressor of G1/S cyclin Whi5 decreased the magnitude of G1 control (sG1 = −0.17 ± 0.02) but compensated with a slight increase in G2/M control (sG2/M = −0.46 ± 0.02, Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Deletion of Whi5 causes a slight increase in G2/M control to sG2/M = -0.46 ± 0.02.
source: We found that deletion of the repressor of G1/S cyclin Whi5 decreased the magnitude of G1 control (sG1 = −0.17 ± 0.02) but compensated with a slight increase in G2/M control (sG2/M = −0.46 ± 0.02, Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The overall size-compensation slope is similar in whi5 and WT cells.
source: However, these changes were relatively modest, and the overall size-compensation slope was similar in whi5 and in WT cells (stot = −0.26 ± 0.03 and stot = −0.22 ± 0.02, respectively; Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: G1 size compensation is slightly improved by deletion of BCK2 with sG1 = -0.34 ± 0.04.
source: However, G1 size compensation was slightly improved by deletion of the activator of G1/S transition BCK2 (sG1 = −0.34 ± 0.04), and the overall compensatory growth was stronger than in WT cells (stot = −0.46 ± 0.06).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: Deletion of sic1, swe1, clb5, and clb2 induces a much larger decrease in size compensation in both G1 and G2/M phases compared to G1/S regulators.
source: In striking contrast to these G1/S regulators, deletion of other cell cycle control genes related to the control of B-type cyclin function, such as sic1, swe1, clb5, and clb2, induced a much larger decrease in size compensation in both G1 and (with the exception of clb2) G2/M phases, as well as the overall compensatory growth (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Loss of Swe1 leads to a slightly Timer-like behavior with stot = 0.15 ± 0.05.
source: For instance, loss of Swe1, which inhibits Cyclin B-Cdk activity and regulates the onset of anaphase, leads to a slightly Timer-like behavior (stot = 0.15 ± 0.05), in which both G1 (sG1 = −0.12 ± 0.03) (Soifer and Barkai, 2014) and G2/M (sG2/M = −0.15 ± 0.04) size compensation were largely abolished.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citation to Soifer and Barkai, 2014.

claim: The Fano factor decreases during G2/M and G1 phases but increases during the rest of the cell cycle, especially during S phase.
source: Still, it displayed some notable variations around the mean at different points in the cell cycle: specifically, F decreased during G2/M and G1 phases, but increased during the rest of the cell cycle, especially during S phase (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Mutants with strong size compensation effects display larger reductions in Fano factor in both G1 and G2/M phases.
source: Importantly, we observed that mutants with strong size compensation effects (i.e. with a negative slope) displayed larger reductions in Fano factor in both G1 and G2/M phases.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data analysis.

claim: The reduction in Fano factor is larger in G2/M (fold-change ~0.65) than in G1 (~0.9) in WT cells.
source: Of interest, the reduction in Fano factor was larger in G2/M (fold-change ~0.65) than in G1 (~0.9) in WT cells (Figure 5B and C), confirming the importance of cell size control during G2/M.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and C.

claim: The magnitude of size compensation mechanisms directly influences size homeostasis in a cell cycle phase-specific manner.
source: Also, this analysis clearly demonstrated that the magnitude of size compensation mechanisms directly influences size homeostasis in a cell cycle phase-specific manner.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on Fano factor changes.

claim: Mutants related to the G1/S network generally display a noise level comparable to WT and lower than mutants associated with the regulation of B-type cyclin function.
source: Interestingly, mutants related to the G1/S network (bck2, swi4, whi5, cln1, with the exception of cln2 and cln3) generally displayed a noise level comparable to WT and lower than did the mutants associated with the regulation of B-type cyclin function (clb5, swe1, clb2, cdh1; Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Fitting the linear map model to experimental data yields an intrinsic noise parameter <η²>/Veq = 3.5 ± 0.5.
source: Fitting the model prediction to the experimental data (using a single parameter fit <η2>/Veq) yielded reasonable agreement, despite a large spread in the experimental data and the existence of an outlier, the dia2 mutant, which failed to fit the model (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by model fitting to experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Convergence rates range from 1.9 × 10^-3 min^-1 to 5.7 × 10^-3 min^-1 across different mutants.
source: By computing λ from p and <Tdiv > , we identified a large spread in convergence rates, ranging from 1.9 × 10−3 min−1 to 5.7 × 10−3 min−1 (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Convergence to equilibrium is impaired in the swe1 mutant compared with WT cells.
source: By selecting the fraction of daughter cells that deviated significantly (larger or smaller) from the equilibrium size at birth and tracking the average size of consecutive daughters, we confirmed that convergence to equilibrium was impaired in the swe1 mutant but slightly improved in the bck2 mutant (yet only for large cells, presumably because the slope p seems different for small versus large bck2 cells on Figure 6A, see above) compared with WT cells (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Convergence to equilibrium is slightly improved in the bck2 mutant for large cells compared with WT cells.
source: By selecting the fraction of daughter cells that deviated significantly (larger or smaller) from the equilibrium size at birth and tracking the average size of consecutive daughters, we confirmed that convergence to equilibrium was impaired in the swe1 mutant but slightly improved in the bck2 mutant (yet only for large cells, presumably because the slope p seems different for small versus large bck2 cells on Figure 6A, see above) compared with WT cells (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The magnitude of bud size compensation during G2/M is comparable to the well-known G1 size control.
source: Building on previous studies (Harvey and Kellogg, 2003), our work now clearly establishes the link between bud growth and cell cycle progression through G2, and reveals that the magnitude of size compensation is comparable to the well-known G1 size control.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data comparing G1 and G2/M size compensation.

claim: Budding and DNA replication are triggered concomitantly by the activation of the G1/S regulon.
source: Although budding and DNA replication are triggered concomitantly by the activation of the G1/S regulon, the noise in bud size that is observed at the end of S phase suggests that these two processes appear to be largely uncoordinated.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about cell cycle regulation.

claim: The function of bud size control during G2/M may be to prevent the potentially deleterious onset of anaphase in small-budded cells following DNA replication.
source: Therefore, the function of bud size control during G2/M may be to prevent the potentially deleterious onset of anaphase in small-budded cells following DNA replication.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observed G2/M size control mechanism.

claim: Mutations of regulators of cyclin B-Cdk activity have a more pronounced effect on cell size homeostasis than mutations of G1 regulators.
source: In contrast, we found that mutations of regulators of cyclin B-Cdk activity had a more pronounced effect on cell size homeostasis: G2/M size compensation was largely abolished in the swe1 mutant (Harvey and Kellogg, 2003), as well as in sic1 and cdh1 mutants.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citation to Harvey and Kellogg, 2003.

claim: G2/M size compensation is largely abolished in the swe1 mutant.
source: In contrast, we found that mutations of regulators of cyclin B-Cdk activity had a more pronounced effect on cell size homeostasis: G2/M size compensation was largely abolished in the swe1 mutant (Harvey and Kellogg, 2003), as well as in sic1 and cdh1 mutants.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citation to Harvey and Kellogg, 2003.

claim: G2/M size compensation is largely abolished in sic1 and cdh1 mutants.
source: In contrast, we found that mutations of regulators of cyclin B-Cdk activity had a more pronounced effect on cell size homeostasis: G2/M size compensation was largely abolished in the swe1 mutant (Harvey and Kellogg, 2003), as well as in sic1 and cdh1 mutants.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: The magnitude of G1 and G2/M size compensations are somewhat coupled across mutant strains.
source: Strikingly, all of these mutations also reduced the magnitude of the G1 size control. With a few notable exceptions (hcm1 or clb2), the fact that the magnitude of G1 and G2/M size compensations are somewhat coupled across these mutant strains suggests that enforcing a clear switch in B-type cyclin-Cdk activity between the low (S/G2/early M) and high (late M/G1) APC activity regimes is critical for cell size homeostasis.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data on multiple mutants.

claim: Enforcing a clear switch in B-type cyclin-Cdk activity between the low and high APC activity regimes is critical for cell size homeostasis.
source: With a few notable exceptions (hcm1 or clb2), the fact that the magnitude of G1 and G2/M size compensations are somewhat coupled across these mutant strains suggests that enforcing a clear switch in B-type cyclin-Cdk activity between the low (S/G2/early M) and high (late M/G1) APC activity regimes is critical for cell size homeostasis.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the observed coupling of G1 and G2/M size compensations.

claim: All strains used in the study were congenic to S288C unless specified otherwise.
source: All strains were congenic to S288C unless specified otherwise and were constructed following standard genetic techniques.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the materials used in the study.

claim: The cdh1Δ HTB2-sfGFP strains were quite unstable and yielded a large fraction of dead cells as well as large multinucleated cells.
source: In the list of constructed strains, we noticed that the cdh1Δ HTB2-sfGFP strains were quite unstable and yielded a large fraction of dead cells as well as large multinucleated cells that retained a fast division time and eventually outgrew the rest of the population.
evidence: This is an observation made during the experimental work.

claim: The cdh1Δ mutation has previously been described to induce genomic instabilities.
source: Indeed, the cdh1Δ mutation has previously been described to induce genomic instabilities (e.g. chromosome loss, etc..)(Ross and Cohen-Fix, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ross and Cohen-Fix, 2003.

claim: Cells were imaged every 3 min using an automated inverted microscope.
source: Cells were imaged every 3 min using an automated inverted microscope (Nikon TI, Nikon, Japan) with a 60 × phase contrast objective and a sCMOS camera (Hamamatsu Orca Flash 4.0, Japan) driven by Nikon Software (NIS).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental methodology.

claim: Cells were allowed to grow for up to 10 hr in the device, yielding about 500 cells per field of view by the end of the assay.
source: The cells were allowed to grow for up to 10 hr in the device, yielding about 500 cells per field of view by the end of the assay.
